France to build 1000km of road with solar panels

Interestingly, this project will not remove road surfaces but instead, the solar panels will be glued to the existing pavement.

Solar, Cement and Glue are best buds, eh? I'm betting Glue is about to stop hanging out when he gets a new girlfriend who goes by 'Tire Treads'.

This is honestly one of the dumbest things I've ever heard. If you're going to go through all the trouble of retrofitting your roads with solar panels why not put the solar panels on some kind of roof above the road, where they aren't getting run over by cars all day, and actually provide some shade for the cars as well.
Which also allows for less intrusion when parts wear out and require replacing. Which would also take much more time than regular road work

I'm guessing that the decision was made on the basis of cost and time. Constructing a roof to me sounds extremely expensive; such a construction would require 1) the materials, 2) the labor, 3) possible maintenance (maybe limited, depending on structural design). Road surface maintenance is already scheduled annually, so from a quick layman's judgment you'd think they were trying to kill two birds with one stone, with the hopes that the installation could coincide with road repair efforts.

And it seems like it's specifically made to support the abuse from cars and trucks. Although I can't help but shake the feeling this was done on purpose in order to hinder the view of solar power to the public's eye when it fails.

I give them credit for trying, maybe they think it wont work but its better than nothing. However I agree this could have been done much more efficiently had they just put the damn things on the SIDE of the road.

I would say it's mainly cost, but hiding them is also important. Think of the cost of the supports, the extra wiring (the roof would need to be tall enough to accommodate trucks), and the hassle that would create for road work crews.
Yeah, that's a good point. It'd be basically a forever tunnel. Maybe not a bad idea for a long term, but a really money consuming one.

That would only be worthwhile if the roadway maintenance costs proved to be higher than building them as a car port. The thermal aspect (heat island) would be the same regardless since no car is going to spend enough time on the road (pending heavy traffic) to actually absorb more sunlight than the road. The road reflectivity would be the same as the car port version for calculation purposes.

Personally I would adopt the carport methodology, but apply it to parking lots since those will hold more heat than the roadways from the simple fact of having a greater surface area, plus with the carport you can significantly reduce your pollution load from stormwater runoff by keeping those parking lots free of water.

Shading the cars when parked would be a nice added benefit.
It would also allow for more light absorption, since you don't have shadows constantly going over it. Watch them put this in a high traffic area, and during rush hour you get brown-outs.
Or don't be a special case and, instead, put the solar panels next to the road.

This is silly...and almost undoubtedly a hoax. The constant wear of vehicles would damage the solar panels in short order, and it would be far less expensive and more durable to put solar panels on top of the roofs of existing buildings, or on an array of freestanding metal poles.

I'm not sure why people are so cynical of this. As the article mentions the Dutch have already successfully carried out a similar experiment. It was only 100 meters of road, but it was a major success. It actually ended up performing better than expected. It turns out about 42 square meters generates enough electricity to cover all electrical needs for a small household. Over there they were designed to support up to 12 ton vehicles and have a life cycle of 20 years. We have millions of miles of road. The math is promising. Laying them on the road is going to be the cheapest, safest, and fastest option.

I think some people have this image of solar as being some sort of weak, fragile, unproductive source of energy. It's not. In reality we could already be running our entire country off of solar and other renewables if not for political and economic hurdles. The fossil fuel industry just has a monstrously powerful lobby, and the price of oil coincidentally falling off a cliff about the time solar really became a viable alternative isn't helping with the transition either.

It's not about how much it can generate, it's about the durability of it from the abuse and how safe it is to drive on.

The Dutch did it on a bike path. Not an actual road.

They did it on a pedestrian road for testing purposes, not to avoid mass. You obviously don't want to have to shut down road with vehicular traffic every time you want to measure, test, tweak, or tune your experiment. The durability is going to be a non issue. Whether something can support a certain level of consistent pressure on it is relatively trivial to ensure. Whether this idea would even technically function was the bigger question and the answer there was a much bigger than expected yes.

This test is the logical progression in the testing process. 1000km sounds like a lot but it's really hardly anything in the grand scheme of things and they're laying it out over 5 years which means they're probably going to do an incremental rollout to minimize cost and resources in case there does need to be a substantial refactoring or rollback.

There's a real chance that right now you're looking at the future of electricity generation on this planet. I find it bemusing that people are mocking it while knowing nothing about it simply because it's not what they're familiar with.

OK, let's say you have two plans for installing an expensive and delicate solar panel that needs to remain unobscured and in direct sunlight to perform at its best.

Plan (A) involves putting it on some kind of raised structure where nothing will cover it in dirt and muck, or scratch up the surface, or cast shadows on it, and it's angled to catch the maximum possible amount of sun.

Plan (B) involves putting it on a piece of flat ground and driving fucking trucks over it.

The vehicles themselves are irrelevant in terms of affect on the insolation. How often do you think any given location of road has a vehicle on top of it? Imagine you say something 'small' like 10%. That would mean if you look at that spot for a day you'd expect to see a vehicle on top of it for 2.4 hours. Let's consider a vehicle that is traveling at a modest highway speed of 50mph and is also huge - about 20 feet long. It's traveling at 73 feet per second. That means it bypasses, from front tire to back, any given point on the road in 0.27 seconds. So how do we get 2.4 hours? You'd need 31,536 vehicles to pass on top of this panel (or 21.9 per minute) just to decrease its exposure by 10%. The only spots where vehicles themselves could affect the insolation would be in locations where traffic comes to a standstill for hours at a time. Although even there imagine you have 5 hours of stand still traffic, that means the panels are still working nominally the other 80% of the time.

Solar panels are not fragile. Versions currently deployed 'bare' are designed to withstand the weather, for instance, hail storms. And these panels will be being deployed with a layer on top of them looking something like this. Although that image is from the company that's deploying them in the US. What you, and I expect most, are underestimating is the power of solar cells. Setting up a solar cell is not like setting up, for instance, satellite TV where if a slight cloud cover comes in or if you're pointed a few degrees off then everything falls to pieces. The technology is already highly productive and efficient. For instance a NASA commissioned MIT study found solar to be the optimal choice for powering a new Mars colony beating out even nuclear for the first time ever. That was obviously factoring in inclimate weather, such as dust storms, on the planet.

Solar doesn't need to be treated like a baby to pump out some serious energy.

The shadowing issue isn't from vehicles (assuming we're not talking about a stretch of road that turns into a parking lot for hours at a time), it's from surrounding structures etc. The much more important issue is the muck and physical wear and tear on the road from traffic. Toughened glass transmits around 90% of light (and hence power) at best when it's brand new. When it's covered in road grime and the surface is scratched to hell by heavy vehicles grinding sand into it all day and night, it's going to transmit far less than that. It's not that it "can't work", it's that it's significantly more expensive than other options per installed kW.

I'm not saying solar is bad or that we shouldn't install it. I've got a stack of panels on my roof that cut my electricity bill by more than 50%, I freaking love solar. I'm just saying that this particular implementation is dumb. Even just installing a strip of panels along the verge on each side of a road would give you the same power output per kilometer of road for a fraction of the cost.

The whole idea behind deploying them on roads is quantity over quality. I don't think many would argue against the fact that there are more 'optimal' locations. However the quantity of those locations tends to pale in comparison to the quantity of roads we have available. The specifics of exactly what sort of output we'll get from highway streets also remains to be seen. You're making a lot of assumptions and I think there's a lot this isn't necessarily intuitive here. At the most basic level there are pretty basic physical solutions to some of the problems you're positing. For instance a material is only capable of scratching another material if it is harder, though it's unclear whether or not surface scratching would even be a meaningful problem in the first place. I'm sure there are also solutions for road gunk. In the absolute worst case scenario there's even relatively basic ideas like developing a zamboni style machine (link if you don't happen to be an ice hockey fan) for highway usage.

Also something you may also not be considering given your focus on the financial side of things here is that in traditional paving once you lay down that road it immediately begins costing you money. With solar cells once you lay down that road it immediately begins making you money. If these experiments end up successful then self sustainability and even 'free expansion' of the roads would not be far away. In our increasingly shaky economy the tons of new jobs this could create would also be a nice perk. And on the topic of perks moving away from fossil fuels is the single most important reason we need to get a project like this going. There's also some nice benefits for the streets themselves having these cells. It opens up the possibility to have streets that can melt ice on their own, could provide signals to drivers today, digitally interweave with the self driving cars of the future, and so on.

Between the dirt, protective layer on the PVs and the far from favourable angle of incidence - I suspect they will run at less than 50% of rated efficiency.
Also, France has the world's lowest CO2 emissions from electricity already. And let's be honest that's not from solar is it?

Sounds like a make work project where the lack of engineering is going to render it useless.

There will be tremendous conversion and transmission losses.

They would be far better off mounting them directly on homes with good insolation.
